title: RSVP-TE: Extensions to RSVP for LSP Tunnels
summary: Extends RSVP so it can set up label-switched paths in MPLS networks. Because traffic on such a path is identified by its label, the paths act like tunnels, which is useful for traffic engineering. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Instead of letting every car pick its own road, this lets a network plan special lanes ahead of time and reserve them for chosen traffic.

questions: how are mpls tunnels set up with rsvp
what is the explicit route object in rsvp-te
how does the rsvp hello extension work
subtitle: How RSVP was extended to build label-switched tunnels along chosen routes in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: MPLS networks need a way to set up label-switched paths along routes the operator or ingress router chooses, optionally with resource reservations, so traffic can be steered away from failures, congestion and bottlenecks.
tldr.mechanism: RSVP gains new objects. The first router's Path message carries a LABEL_REQUEST and optionally an EXPLICIT_ROUTE, and the Resv message coming back upstream carries a LABEL object that each hop uses to bind labels.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and the base specification for RSVP-TE tunnels. Later RFCs update it, including RFC 3936, RFC 4420, RFC 4874, RFC 5151, RFC 5420, RFC 5711, RFC 6780, RFC 6790 and RFC 7274.

today: RFC 3209 is a Proposed Standard, and it has been updated by RFC 3936, RFC 4420, RFC 4874, RFC 5151, RFC 5420, RFC 5711, RFC 6780, RFC 6790 and RFC 7274. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why RSVP Was Extended for MPLS
sections.content:
RFC 3209 specifies extensions to RSVP (the Resource Reservation Protocol) so it can establish label switched paths (LSPs) in MPLS networks. The MPLS architecture does not assume a single label distribution protocol, and this document is one such protocol. Many of its features were motivated by the needs of traffic engineering over MPLS, described in RFC 2702.

Because the traffic on an LSP is identified by the label applied at the ingress node, the path can be treated as a tunnel that runs below normal IP routing and filtering. The RFC calls this an LSP tunnel. Such tunnels can be routed away from failures, congestion and bottlenecks, and several parallel tunnels can be set up between two nodes.

The extended protocol supports explicitly routed LSPs with or without resource reservations, smooth rerouting, preemption and loop detection. It also adds a Hello message for quick node failure detection. The discussion is limited to unicast LSPs; multicast LSPs are left for further study.
sections.eli5: A network can set up a private lane for some traffic. Once the lane exists, cars only need to follow the lane markings, and the planners can send the lane around traffic jams.

sections.title: LSP Tunnels and TE Tunnels
sections.content:
Standard RSVP defines a session as a data flow with a particular destination and transport-layer protocol. With MPLS, a flow can be defined much more flexibly: the ingress node can use any means it likes to decide which packets get a given label, and the label then defines the flow through the LSP. Intermediate nodes see the traffic as opaque.

New C-Types for the SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC objects, called LSP_TUNNEL_IPv4 and LSP_TUNNEL_IPv6, support this. A node on the path identifies tunnel traffic solely by the label it assigned to upstream senders.

Two identifiers tie related tunnels together. The Tunnel ID in the SESSION object uniquely defines a traffic engineered tunnel (TE tunnel), which is a set of one or more LSP tunnels carrying a traffic trunk. The LSP ID in the SENDER_TEMPLATE or FILTER_SPEC, together with the SESSION object, identifies one particular LSP tunnel.
sections.eli5: A tunnel has a name that stays the same for its whole life, and each version of it gets its own ticket number. That way the network can tell the old route from the new route of the same tunnel.

sections.title: Setting Up an LSP Tunnel
sections.content:
To create a tunnel, the first MPLS node on the path builds an RSVP Path message with a session type of LSP_TUNNEL_IPv4 or LSP_TUNNEL_IPv6 and adds a LABEL_REQUEST object. The request also says which network layer protocol will be carried, because it cannot be assumed to be IP. The sender may add an EXPLICIT_ROUTE object to name the route it wants.

The destination answers with a Resv message that contains a LABEL object. The Resv message travels back upstream along the reverse of the path state created by the Path message. Each node that receives a LABEL uses it for outgoing traffic on this tunnel. If the node is not the sender, it allocates a new label and puts it in the LABEL object it sends to the previous hop. That label is the one the node will use to identify incoming traffic, and the node updates its Incoming Label Map. When the Resv reaches the sender, the LSP is established.

A LABEL carries a single label in 4 octets. A generic MPLS label is an unsigned integer from 0 through 1048575. A receiver that accepts a LABEL_REQUEST MUST include a LABEL in its Resv messages, and a node MUST NOT include a LABEL if no LABEL_REQUEST was present. Labels are allocated downstream, on demand.

All the new objects are OPTIONAL with respect to RSVP, but LABEL_REQUEST and LABEL are mandatory for this specification. A router that does not recognise an object answers with an "Unknown object class" error and the setup fails.
sections.eli5: The first router sends a note down the road asking for a lane number. The last router answers, and the answer travels back, with every router on the way writing down which lane number it will use.

sections.title: Explicit Routes and Recorded Routes
sections.content:
The EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (ERO, class 20) is a series of subobjects. Each one names an abstract node, which is a group of nodes whose inner topology is opaque to the ingress. The defined subobject types are 1 (IPv4 prefix), 2 (IPv6 prefix) and 32 (autonomous system number). An abstract node can therefore be a single router, an address prefix or a whole autonomous system.

An L bit in each subobject marks it as loose when set and strict when clear. Between a strict node and its predecessor the path MUST contain only nodes from those two abstract nodes. For a loose node, other nodes may appear in between. Each router processes the first subobject, picks a next hop, and may rewrite the list before forwarding. Errors include "Bad initial subobject", "Bad strict node" and "Bad loose node".

The RECORD_ROUTE object (RRO, class 21) collects the actual route hop by hop. Each router adds its own address to the top of a last-in-first-out list of subobjects (IPv4 address, IPv6 address, or Label). The RRO serves three purposes: loop detection, learning the real path, and feeding the result back into an ERO to pin a path down. If a router finds its own address already in the list, a forwarding loop exists, and it sends a "Routing problem" PathErr with the value "loop detected" and drops the Path message.
sections.eli5: The explicit route is a list of towns the trip must go through. Some stops are strict, meaning go straight there, and some are loose, meaning take any road you like. The record route is a trail of breadcrumbs that shows which way the trip really went.

sections.title: Rerouting Without Breaking the Tunnel
sections.content:
Operators need to reroute a TE tunnel when a better route appears or a resource fails, without disrupting traffic. The RFC describes make-before-break: build the new LSP tunnel first, move the traffic onto it, then tear down the old one. The trouble is that the old and new tunnels may compete for the same bandwidth on shared links, and admission control could refuse the new one. Counting the reservation twice must be avoided.

The solution combines the LSP_TUNNEL SESSION object with the Shared Explicit (SE) reservation style. The ingress keeps the same SESSION (same Tunnel ID and Extended Tunnel ID) but picks a new LSP ID, forms a new SENDER_TEMPLATE and ERO, and sends a new Path message. It keeps refreshing both old and new Path messages. On shared links the two reservations share resources. When the Resv for the new path arrives, the ingress moves traffic to it and SHOULD send a PathTear for the old route.

The same trick works for increasing bandwidth: a new LSP ID is used to attempt the larger reservation while the old one continues to be refreshed, so the existing reservation is not lost if the larger request fails.
sections.eli5: To switch roads, you build the new road first and only close the old road once the new one is open. The two roads are allowed to share the same lanes where they overlap, so nobody gets stuck.

sections.title: Priorities, Flags and Resource Affinities
sections.content:
The SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object (class 207) helps with identification, diagnostics and policy. It carries a Setup Priority and a Holding Priority, each from 0 to 7 with 0 the highest. Setup priority decides whether a new session may preempt another, and holding priority decides whether an existing session can be preempted. The setup priority SHOULD never be higher than the holding priority. A human-readable session name is included.

Three flags are defined: 0x01 local protection desired, 0x02 label recording desired, and 0x04 SE style desired. The label recording flag asks nodes to include a Label subobject in the RRO.

A second C-Type (LSP_TUNNEL_RA) adds three 32-bit vectors: Exclude-any, Include-any and Include-all. A link must pass all three tests against its own attribute bits to be acceptable. If no acceptable link can be found to extend a loose ERO node, the router SHOULD send a "Routing Problem" PathErr with the value "no route available toward destination".
sections.eli5: Each tunnel gets a number saying how important it is. A more important tunnel can bump a less important one. It can also say which roads it refuses to use and which it insists on.

sections.title: The Hello Extension
sections.content:
The Hello extension lets RSVP neighbours notice when a neighbour node is no longer reachable. It is aimed at cases where the link layer does not report failures quickly enough. It is completely OPTIONAL, and one side can use it while the other does not.

It consists of a Hello message (message type 20), a HELLO REQUEST object (C-Type 1) and a HELLO ACK object (C-Type 2) in the HELLO class, 22. Both objects carry a 32-bit Src_Instance and a 32-bit Dst_Instance. The Src_Instance MUST change when the sender resets, reboots or loses contact, and MUST NOT be zero. A node treats a neighbour as lost if the instance value changes, if the neighbour reflects a wrong value back, or if nothing is received within a configured number of hello intervals. The text gives a default of 3.5 intervals and a default hello_interval of 5 ms.

Hello messages go between immediate neighbours, so the IP TTL SHOULD be 1. A request sent to a neighbour that does not support the extension simply goes unanswered.
sections.eli5: Neighbours keep checking, "Are you still there?" Each one has a secret number that changes if it restarts, so if the number changes, the other knows it rebooted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says these extensions pose no security exposure beyond RFC 2205, with one change to the trust model. On a normal RSVP session, traffic can be filtered by source and destination addresses and ports. With LSP tunnels, filtering happens only on the incoming label.

An administration may therefore want to limit the domain in which LSP tunnels can be established. The RFC suggests doing this by setting filters that deny RSVP Path messages carrying a SESSION object of type LSP_TUNNEL_IPv4 (7) or LSP_TUNNEL_IPv6 (8).
sections.eli5: Since the lane markings alone decide who gets in, a network owner may want to decide ahead of time who is allowed to paint new lane markings.
